citeAs: Masry, Ahmed, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, and Enamul Hoque. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
description: ChartQA is a large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts that covers human-authored and machine-generated question-answer pairs over real-world charts, focusing on visual and logical reasoning. It contains 20,882 charts curated from four online sources, with 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 questions generated from human-written chart summaries.
name: ChartQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 questions per chart were written by one worker, and the same questions were answered by another annotator.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers on Amazon Mechanical Turk; workers were selected with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs, and were further filtered with a pre-test.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human-authored QA pairs, the same questions were answered by another annotator. If both workers’ answers exactly matched, the answer was accepted; otherwise the authors manually checked the answers to select the final correct answer. Exact-match agreement was 61.04%, and manual checking on 500 random samples found 78.55% agreement when considering typos and lexical variations.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For human-authored QA pairs, the authors designed an AMT task asking crowdworkers to focus on compositional and visual questions for each chart image. For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers; the same questions were then answered by another annotator, and disagreements were manually resolved. Workers were selected with a 95% acceptance rate, at least 5000 HITs, and a pre-test.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is built from four online sources to ensure variety in visual styles and topics, but politics is a common topic across all sources and nearly half of Pew charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). The machine-generated questions come only from Statista human-written summaries, and the filtering heuristic retains generated questions only when the answer can be found in the chart data table, biasing generated questions toward chart-element values and labels.
rai:dataCollection: The authors crawled charts from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World in Data, and OECD. For Pew they crawled only chart images because underlying data tables were unavailable; for the other three they extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions, and extracted bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the Pew dataset, the authors only crawled chart images because the underlying data tables were not available.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw/source data included real-world chart images from Statista, Pew Research, Our World in Data, and OECD. For three sources the collected materials also included underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions.
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark is more challenging than previous datasets because of human-written visual and logical reasoning questions, and model performance remains substantially below perfect. The paper also notes that automatic data extraction from real-world charts is error-prone, performance is lower when gold tables are not provided, and pie and line charts are harder due to extraction errors.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset includes machine-generated augmentation: the authors generated 23,111 questions from human-written Statista chart summaries using two fine-tuned T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation. They filtered invalid generated questions with a heuristic that removed questions whose answers could not be found in the chart data table, and manually cleaned the machine-generated test set by removing invalid questions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For collected charts, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, associated text descriptions, and bounding boxes of chart elements from SVG files. They randomly split both ChartQA-H and ChartQA-M into train, validation, and test sets. For machine-generated questions, they filtered out invalid questions if the answer could not be found in the chart data table and manually cleaned the machine-generated test set by removing invalid questions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper notes that the models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. It also discusses ethical considerations including respecting source intellectual property, fairly compensating Mechanical Turk annotators, and anonymizing annotator data to protect privacy.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark for chart question answering, especially for evaluating systems on visual and logical reasoning over real-world charts. The paper states that a ChartQA system can help users by taking a chart and a natural language question as input and predicting the answer.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 models were used to automatically generate machine-generated QA pairs from human-written chart summaries: one model for answer extraction and another for answer-aware question generation. CRAFT was used to recognize chart text and ChartOCR was adapted to extract structured data tables from chart images.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No personal sensitive information from annotators was released; annotations were anonymized to protect worker privacy.
